title: Service & Business Logic Architecture
readme:
FULL-STACK DEVELOPER 2026
Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

This phase continues the validated, persistent, professionally error-handled Task API from Phase 13.
It teaches controller/service boundaries, business invariants, Task workflow policy, cross-model membership rules, business validation, transaction reasoning, and extraction thresholds without premature Repository Pattern or Clean Architecture layers.

Course locks remain:
- NestJS 12.0.3
- Fastify 5.x course line
- Prisma 7.9.1
- Zod 4.6.5

Start with 00_Phase_14_Guide.pdf or 11_Phase_14_Complete_Book.pdf.
The reference snapshot contains only Phase 14 changed/emphasized files and assumes Phase 13 is already complete.

lessons.body:
Controller vs Service Responsibilities
Keep HTTP translation thin while providers execute application use cases

Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

HTTP request

v

Controller

v

TasksService

v

PrismaService

Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple.

A controller translates HTTP; a service executes a use case
NestJS documentation recommends that controllers handle HTTP requests and delegate more complex work to
providers. TaskFlow now makes that separation concrete: controllers translate transport concerns; TasksService
owns Task use cases and rules.

Controller owns                                                   TasksService owns

route + HTTP method                                               business workflow

path/body extraction                                              domain invariants

validation pipe invocation                                        cross-model checks

status semantics                                                  orchestration of reads/writes

delegate to provider                                              meaningful application exceptions

Thin does not mean useless
A controller still has an important responsibility: it defines the transport contract. Thin means it does not decide
whether DONE can return to TODO, whether an assignee belongs to a workspace, or how completedAt should
change.

@Patch(":id")
update(
@Param("id", { schema: taskIdSchema }) id: string,
@Body(new StandardSchemaValidationPipe(updateTaskSchema)) input: UpdateTaskDto,
) {
return this.tasksService.update(id, input);
}

Figure 1 - Use-case ownership

HTTP PATCH /tasks/:id

v

Controller validates/extracts transport data

v

TasksService evaluates Task rules

v

PrismaService persists valid state

The service is where transport-independent application meaning lives.

Service layer is not a pass-through layer
If TasksService only forwards every input directly to prisma.task.update(), it is not protecting business behavior. As
rules appear, the service should coordinate the use case before the write.

Avoid controller business logic

Putting transition tables or membership queries into TasksController makes the same rules difficult to reuse from jobs, tests,
CLI tools, or future non-HTTP entry points.

The opposite anti-pattern: god service

A service can also grow too large. Do not respond by extracting arbitrary classes early. First group methods by use
case and keep private rule helpers local. Extract only when a rule becomes independently complex, reused, or
deserves its own clear responsibility.

lessons.body:
Business Invariants & Rule Ownership
Separate transport validation, business rules, authorization, and database constraints

Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

Request shape

v

Application invariant

v

Database integrity

Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple.

Invariant: a rule that must remain true
A business invariant is a statement the application should protect across valid operations. It is different from a
TypeScript type, a request shape, and often different from a database constraint.

Rule                                                                  Best first owner

title is a string <= 200 chars                                        Zod boundary

projectId references an existing row                                  PostgreSQL FK + service-friendly 404

assignee belongs to Project workspace                                 TasksService

DONE sets completedAt                                                 TasksService

workspaceId + userId unique                                           PostgreSQL unique constraint

caller may edit this Task                                             authorization layer later

Why some rules cannot be expressed as simple database constraints
The assignee rule crosses Task -> Project -> Workspace and Membership. PostgreSQL can ensure assigneeId
references a real User, but the current model does not encode the stronger rule that the User must also belong to the
Task workspace. The application service therefore checks that invariant.

Figure 1 - Assignee invariant

Task belongs to Project

v

Project belongs to Workspace

v

Candidate User

v

Membership(workspaceId,userId) must exist

v

Only then assign Task

A valid foreign key is necessary but not sufficient for this business rule.

Validation layers complement one another
Layer                                 Question

Zod                                   Is assigneeId shaped like a UUID?

TasksService                          Is that User a member of this Workspace?

PostgreSQL                            Does that User row actually exist?

Do not make Zod query the database

Request schema validation should stay deterministic and focused on shape/format. Database-dependent business rules
belong in application logic, not inside the transport schema.

lessons.title: Task Status Workflow and Derived State
lessons.summary: Task Status Workflow & Derived State Explicit transitions, completedAt consistency, and operations with business meaning Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Current Task status v Transition policy v Derived state v Persist Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented…
lessons.body:
Task Status Workflow & Derived State
Explicit transitions, completedAt consistency, and operations with business meaning

Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

Current Task status

v

Transition policy

v

Derived state

v

Persist

Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple.

Model Task status as a workflow, not a free-form field
Zod can prove that a status value is one of TODO, IN_PROGRESS, DONE, or CANCELED. It cannot decide whether
a specific transition is allowed from the current persisted state. That requires reading the Task and applying workflow
policy.

const ALLOWED_STATUS_TRANSITIONS = {
TODO:        [IN_PROGRESS, CANCELED],
IN_PROGRESS: [TODO, DONE, CANCELED],
DONE:        [IN_PROGRESS],
CANCELED:    [TODO],
};

From                              Allowed next states

TODO                              IN_PROGRESS, CANCELED

IN_PROGRESS                       TODO, DONE, CANCELED

DONE                              IN_PROGRESS

CANCELED                          TODO

Figure 1 - Status transition reasoning

Read current status

v

Requested status differs?

v

Check transition policy

v

Reject invalid transition with 409

v

Apply derived side effects

v

Persist valid update

The update becomes an application operation, not an arbitrary column assignment.

Derived state: completedAt
When Task status changes to DONE, TaskFlow records completedAt. When a DONE Task is reopened, completedAt
is cleared. That makes status and completion timestamp internally consistent.

if (to === TaskStatus.DONE) return new Date();
if (from === TaskStatus.DONE) return null;

Why not let the frontend set completedAt?

The client may request a business action such as completing a Task, but the server owns the authoritative timestamp and
invariant. Otherwise clients can create contradictory states such as status=TODO with completedAt populated.

CRUD field update vs business operation
PATCH remains a valid transport for this phase, but TasksService interprets status as a workflow change rather than
blindly forwarding it. In larger domains, an explicit operation such as POST /purchase-orders/:id/approve can be
clearer than a generic field patch because approval has business meaning and side effects.

lessons.title: Cross Model Rules and Workspace Membership
lessons.summary: Cross-Model Rules & Workspace Membership Use relational context to enforce assignee membership invariants Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Task Project v Workspace v Membership v Assignment Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application…
lessons.body:
Cross-Model Rules & Workspace
Membership
Use relational context to enforce assignee membership invariants

Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

Task Project

v

Workspace

v

Membership

v

Assignment

Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple.

Cross-model business rules require context
An assigneeId is not valid merely because the User exists. The Task Project determines a Workspace, and the User
must have a Membership in that Workspace.

const project = await prisma.project.findUnique({
where: { id: input.projectId },
select: { id: true, workspaceId: true },
});

const membership = await prisma.membership.findUnique({
where: {
workspaceId_userId: {
workspaceId: project.workspaceId,
userId: input.assigneeId,
},
},
});

The composite unique key becomes useful
Phase 10 intentionally defined @@unique([workspaceId, userId]). That schema design now gives the service an
unambiguous and efficient way to ask whether this exact membership exists.

Figure 1 - Cross-model rule

Task / Project context

v

workspaceId

v

candidate assigneeId

v

Membership lookup using workspaceId_userId

v

Membership exists -> assignment allowed

v

No membership -> 409 business conflict

The service composes relational facts into an application rule.

A 409 is more useful than a database crash
ASSIGNEE_NOT_WORKSPACE_MEMBER is a deliberate business conflict: the request is syntactically valid, the
User may exist, but the requested state conflicts with TaskFlow workspace rules.

Authentication is still later

This check does not ask whether the current caller is allowed to assign the Task. That is authorization and arrives later. Phase
14 only proves the target assignee satisfies the Task domain invariant.

lessons.title: Business Validation and Time Based Policies
lessons.summary: Business Validation & Time-Based Policies Why semantically valid state needs more than Zod request validation Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Valid timestamp v Business clock/policy v Accept or reject Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods…
lessons.body:
Business Validation & Time-Based
Policies
Why semantically valid state needs more than Zod request validation

Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

Valid timestamp

v

Business clock/policy

v

Accept or reject

Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple.

Business validation is not the same as transport validation
Phase 12 protects the request boundary. Phase 14 protects the application state. These validations run at different
moments and answer different questions.

Question                                                Layer                              Example response

Is dueAt a valid ISO datetime?                          Zod                                400 BAD_REQUEST

Does this course allow a new past due date?             TasksService                       400 DUE_DATE_IN_PAST

Does projectId exist?                                   TasksService + DB                  404 PROJECT_NOT_FOUND

Is assigneeId a UUID?                                   Zod                                400 BAD_REQUEST

Is assignee a Workspace member?                         TasksService                       409 ASSIGNEE_NOT_WORKSPACE_M
EMBER

A policy may use current time
A due-date-in-the-past rule depends on application meaning and the current clock. It is not just a string-format rule.
The service therefore parses the already validated timestamp and compares it with the current time.

private assertDueDate(dueAt?: string | null): void {
if (!dueAt) return;
if (new Date(dueAt).getTime() < Date.now()) {
throw new DueDateInPastException();
}
}

Be careful with clocks
Time-based business rules eventually deserve a controllable Clock dependency in heavily tested domains. We do
not introduce that abstraction yet because formal unit testing and time simulation arrive later. The book calls out the
trade-off so the learner understands why Date.now() may later become a seam.

Do not duplicate the same rule everywhere

If the frontend also warns about past dates, that improves UX, but the backend remains authoritative. Client validation is
convenience; server business logic protects the system.

lessons.title: Prisma Transactions and Atomic Workflows
lessons.summary: Prisma Transactions & Atomic Workflows Choose nested writes, transaction arrays, or interactive transactions only when a use case needs them Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Business operation v Dependent DB steps v Transaction boundary v…
lessons.body:
Prisma Transactions & Atomic Workflows
Choose nested writes, transaction arrays, or interactive transactions only when a use case needs
them

Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

Business operation

v

Dependent DB steps

v

Transaction boundary

v

Commit or rollback

Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple.

Transactions protect one business operation across multiple
database steps
A transaction is appropriate when a use case must treat multiple dependent reads/writes as one unit. Prisma 7
supports nested writes, sequential $transaction([...]), and interactive $transaction(async tx => ...).

Scenario                                               Transaction?                        Reason

Update one Task title                                  No extra transaction                One Prisma update is already atomic

Create Task row only                                   No extra transaction                Single write

Create parent + related rows                           Nested write can provide            Dependent writes
transactional behavior

Check membership then assign as one workflow           Interactive transaction can group   Read/check then write
the workflow

Two unrelated read queries for a dashboard             Usually no                          Atomicity may not be required

return this.prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {
const task = await tx.task.findUnique(...);
const membership = await tx.membership.findUnique(...);

if (!membership) {
throw new AssigneeNotWorkspaceMemberException(assigneeId);
}

return tx.task.update({
where: { id },
data: { assigneeId },
});
});

Keep interactive transactions short
Do not call slow external APIs, wait for user input, or perform long CPU work inside an interactive transaction. The
database resources remain tied to that transaction while the callback is running.

Transaction does not automatically solve every concurrency problem

Isolation level and retry strategy still matter for strict concurrent invariants. Phase 14 introduces transaction scope; deeper
concurrency control belongs later. Do not claim that wrapping arbitrary code in $transaction makes all race conditions
impossible.

Use the transaction client inside the callback
Queries that belong to the transaction must use tx, not the outer PrismaService. This is why the membership helper
accepts either PrismaService or Prisma.TransactionClient in the reference snapshot.

Service Orchestration & Extraction
Thresholds
Keep logic readable and know when complexity has earned a new abstraction

Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

Load context

v

Check rules

v

Derive state

v

Persist

v

Extract only with evidence

Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple.

Orchestration means coordinating steps for one use case
A service method can read context, check invariants, calculate derived state, then persist. That sequence is
application orchestration. It is different from merely writing raw database queries.

Figure 1 - Update Task orchestration

Load current Task state

v

Validate due-date business policy

v

Validate status transition

v

Validate assignee membership if supplied

v

Derive completedAt

v

Persist update

v

Return result

The order of operations communicates the use case clearly.

Keep private helpers close until complexity earns extraction
private assertStatusTransition(...)
private completedAtForTransition(...)
private assertDueDate(...)
private assertWorkspaceMembership(...)

These helpers make the service readable without inventing TaskPolicyService, TaskDomainService,
TaskRulesEngine, or a dozen interfaces. If they later become complex, reused, or independently testable, extraction
can become justified.

Signal                                                      Possible next step

One private helper, used once                               Keep local

Several pure transition rules growing together              Consider Task workflow/policy object later

Same rule used by multiple services                         Consider shared provider with one clear responsibility

Database access duplicated everywhere                       Repository pattern may eventually earn its place

Different bounded domains changing independently            Revisit module boundaries

Architecture grows from pressure

Do not predict every future abstraction. Let repeated complexity create evidence for the next design move.

lessons.summary: Anti-Patterns & Architecture Theater Avoid controller business logic, blind Prisma patches, transaction-everywhere, and premature layers Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture Volume 04 - Professional Backend Architecture milestone Simple architecture v Pressure appears v Add only needed structure Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service…

Anti-Patterns & Architecture Theater
Avoid controller business logic, blind Prisma patches, transaction-everywhere, and premature
layers

Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

Simple architecture

v

Pressure appears

v

Add only needed structure

Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple.

Common business-layer anti-patterns
The fastest way to understand the service layer is to see what happens when responsibilities leak.

Anti-pattern 1 - Controller performs database queries
@Patch(":id")
async update(...) {
const task = await this.prisma.task.findUnique(...);
// business checks here
return this.prisma.task.update(...);
}

This couples HTTP handling directly to persistence and makes the use case harder to reuse.

Anti-pattern 2 - Prisma update object becomes the business model
return prisma.task.update({
where: { id },
data: input, // every valid field is treated as a legal business transition
});

Request-shape validity does not mean every state transition is allowed.

Anti-pattern 3 - Error filter decides business meaning
Phase 13 already established that the global filter formats errors. It should not infer Task workflow rules from URLs or
Prisma codes.

Anti-pattern 4 - transaction everywhere
Wrapping every single Prisma operation in $transaction adds complexity without improving atomicity. One database
write already succeeds or fails atomically.

Anti-pattern 5 - Clean Architecture cosplay
TaskController
-> TaskUseCaseFacade
-> TaskApplicationService
-> TaskDomainService
-> TaskRepositoryInterface
-> PrismaTaskRepository
-> TaskMapper
-> Prisma

More layers are not automatically more professional

Use layers because they isolate a real kind of change or complexity. At TaskFlow's current scale, Controller -> TasksService
-> PrismaService is still an excellent architecture.

Anti-pattern 6 - service knows HTTP framework details
TasksService should throw meaningful application exceptions, not manipulate Fastify Reply or manually construct
transport responses. That keeps business behavior reusable outside HTTP.

lessons.body:
Enterprise Transfer
Map the service-layer mental model to HRIS, payroll, procurement, inventory, and recruitment

Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

Entry point

v

Application service

v

Business workflow

v

Persistence

Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple.

How this service architecture scales to enterprise systems
The same reasoning transfers to domains that are more serious than Tasks. The names change; the separation of
responsibilities remains useful.

Domain                                 Example application-service rule

HRIS Leave                             Employee cannot consume more leave than policy allows

Payroll                                Payroll run cannot be finalized twice

Procurement                            Purchase order cannot be approved before required approvals

Inventory                              Stock transfer cannot reduce source stock below allowed level

Recruitment                            Applicant cannot move to hired before required screening state

Figure 1 - Enterprise transfer

HTTP / job / command entry point

v

Application service

v

Business invariants + workflow

v

Transaction when operation spans dependent writes

v

Persistence

The service layer is valuable because domain rules survive changes in transport and UI.

A service method should read like a business use case
Names such as finalizePayrollRun(), approvePurchaseOrder(), transferStock(), and submitLeaveRequest()
communicate more than generic update() when the operation has domain meaning and multiple rules.

CRUD remains appropriate for simple resources
Do not replace all CRUD methods with ceremonial verbs. A simple profile description update may remain
updateProfile(). A multi-step approval workflow deserves a richer use-case method. Choose based on behavior, not
fashion.

From Todo tutorial to software engineering

The important shift is that the database no longer defines the application. Persistent rows support the domain; application
services decide which state changes are meaningful and allowed.

lessons.body:
Hands-On Lab & Phase Exit
Workflow rules, membership invariant, transaction reasoning, exercises, and oral exam

Phase 14 - Service & Business Logic Architecture
Volume 04 - Professional Backend

Architecture milestone

Implement

v

Verify state

v

Explain boundaries

v

Transfer skill

Phase 14 turns CRUD-oriented service methods into explicit application rules and workflows while keeping infrastructure simple.

Hands-on lab
This lab proves that TaskFlow now protects business state, not only request shape.

Lab A - Status workflow
• Implement ALLOWED_STATUS_TRANSITIONS in TasksService.

• Reject a transition that is not in the policy.

• Set completedAt when moving into DONE.

• Clear completedAt when reopening DONE.

• Verify the persisted row after each operation.

Lab B - Workspace assignment invariant
• Add assigneeId to write DTOs as optional/nullable UUID.

• Load the Task Project workspace context.

• Verify Membership(workspaceId,userId) exists before assignment.

• Return ASSIGNEE_NOT_WORKSPACE_MEMBER for a syntactically valid non-member.

• Verify unassigning with null succeeds.

Lab C - Transaction reasoning
• Implement the explicit /tasks/:id/assignee workflow from the snapshot.

• Use tx for every Prisma query inside the interactive transaction.

• Explain why update-title does not need the same extra transaction.

• Identify one future enterprise operation that would require several dependent writes.

Lab D - Smoke matrix
Scenario                                                             Expected

TODO -> IN_PROGRESS                                                  Success

IN_PROGRESS -> DONE                                                  Success + completedAt populated

DONE -> IN_PROGRESS                                                  Success + completedAt cleared

DONE -> TODO directly                                                409 TASK_STATUS_TRANSITION_NOT_ALLOWED

assign Workspace member                                              Success

assign non-member                                                    409 ASSIGNEE_NOT_WORKSPACE_MEMBER

set new due date in past                                             400 DUE_DATE_IN_PAST

set dueAt null                                                       Success; due date cleared

Exercise levels
Level                      Challenge

1 - Follow                 Implement the reference rules and pass the PowerShell smoke checks.

2 - Modify                 Add a rule that CANCELED Tasks cannot receive a new assignee until restored to TODO.

Level                      Challenge

3 - Implement              Create a changeStatus(id,targetStatus) service method and make generic update delegate status changes
through it.

4 - Engineer               Design an approvePurchaseOrder() workflow with at least four invariants and identify exactly which steps must be
transactional. Do not write code until the responsibilities are mapped.

Architecture oral exam
• Why does Zod not own the assignee membership rule?

• Why should completedAt be server-derived?

• When is a single Prisma write enough without $transaction?

• Why does a controller delegate workflow decisions to a service?

• What evidence would justify extracting Task transition rules into another provider?

• How is a business invariant different from a database foreign key?

• Why is authorization not the same as membership-validity business logic?

Phase exit checklist
• controllers remain thin and transport-focused.

• TasksService protects explicit Task workflow rules.

• invalid status transitions produce stable business errors.

• completedAt stays consistent with DONE/reopen behavior.

• Task assignees must belong to the Task workspace.

• business validation is distinct from Zod shape validation.

• transactions are used intentionally, not automatically.

• no Repository Pattern or unnecessary architecture layers were introduced.

• you can map the same service-layer reasoning to HRIS, payroll, procurement, and inventory use cases.

Figure 1 - Phase 14 complete architecture

HTTP request

v

Controller = transport

v

TasksService = use case + invariants

v

PrismaService / transaction when justified

v

PostgreSQL = durable integrity

TaskFlow now has a real application-service layer instead of database-driven CRUD.

Next phase

Phase 15 adds Filtering, Search, Sorting & Pagination. We will design query parameters, safe dynamic Prisma filters,
pagination trade-offs, index-aware access patterns, query DTOs, metadata, and API contracts for collection endpoints.

Guided Build Lab — Phase 14: Service & Business Logic Architecture

Purpose
Move orchestration and business invariants into cohesive services/policies so transport and persistence details do not become the domain model.

Deliverable
Refactored task service with explicit policies/invariants and thin controllers.

Before you touch the code
Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything.

Architecture trace
validated request -> service use case -> policy/invariant -> repository/Prisma -> result/error

Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization.

Step 1 — Choose one endpoint with mixed concerns and list every responsibility it currently performs.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 2 — Move HTTP-only concerns back to controller/boundary and persistence mechanics behind a focused collaborator.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. Step 3 — Express one business rule with a name that describes the rule, not the framework.

Step 5 — Test the rule without booting the whole web server where practical.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 6 — Review the resulting dependency direction and remove abstractions that add no clarity.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Checkpoint
When the lab works, inspect git diff. Remove accidental debugging output and unrelated edits. Run type checking/tests/build commands relevant to this phase. Commit the checkpoint with a message that describes the capability added, not merely the files changed.

Explain-back
Without looking at the lesson, explain why each layer in the architecture trace exists, what this phase added to TaskFlow, and what would break if the new responsibility were moved to the wrong layer. If you cannot explain the boundary, repeat the trace before moving on.

lessons.summary:
Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.
lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 14: Service & Business Logic Architecture

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
validated request -> service use case -> policy/invariant -> repository/Prisma -> result/error

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — God services with hundreds of unrelated lines
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Business rules duplicated in controllers and frontend
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

lessons.title: Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge
lessons.summary:
Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 14 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?
lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Service & Business Logic Architecture

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 14 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Move orchestration and business invariants into cohesive services/policies so transport and persistence details do not become the domain model.

Required artifact
Refactored task service with explicit policies/invariants and thin controllers.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can place a rule in the correct layer.
• Can keep controllers thin.
• Can explain orchestration vs persistence.
• Can refactor without changing external behavior.

Independent build sequence
1. Choose one endpoint with mixed concerns and list every responsibility it currently performs.
2. Move HTTP-only concerns back to controller/boundary and persistence mechanics behind a focused collaborator.
3. Express one business rule with a name that describes the rule, not the framework.
4. Add a use-case method whose inputs/outputs make orchestration visible.
5. Test the rule without booting the whole web server where practical.
6. Review the resulting dependency direction and remove abstractions that add no clarity.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

lessons.title: Mastery Capstone Lab
lessons.summary: Integrate Phase 14 without following a transcript.
lessons.body:
Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 14: Service & Business Logic Architecture. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
Refactored task service with explicit policies/invariants and thin controllers.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

objectives: Move orchestration and business invariants into cohesive services/policies so transport and persistence details do not become the domain model.
Produce a reproducible evidence packet for success and failure.

Test the rule without booting the whole web server where practical.
Review the resulting dependency direction and remove abstractions that add no clarity.

references.preview:
TaskFlow Phase 14 reference snapshot

This snapshot contains only the files changed or emphasized by Phase 14. It assumes the completed Phase 13 project already exists.

Core rules demonstrated:
- Controllers remain thin and delegate use cases to TasksService.
- TasksService owns Task business invariants.
- Task status changes follow an explicit transition policy.
- completedAt is synchronized with DONE/reopen transitions.
- A Task assignee must be a member of the Task Project's Workspace.
- New due dates cannot be in the past (course policy for this application).
- A transaction is used for the explicit assignment workflow because the operation reads membership context and then writes the assignment as one use case.
- We do not introduce Repository Pattern yet; PrismaService remains the persistence boundary for this phase.

# Phase 14 business-rule smoke checks.
# Replace placeholders with IDs from your development seed/database.

$api = "http://127.0.0.1:4000"
$taskId = "<TASK_UUID>"
$workspaceMemberUserId = "<MEMBER_USER_UUID>"
$nonMemberUserId = "<NON_MEMBER_USER_UUID>"

# Allowed transition: TODO -> IN_PROGRESS
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Patch `
  -Uri "$api/tasks/$taskId" `
  -ContentType "application/json" `
  -Body '{"status":"IN_PROGRESS"}'

# Allowed transition: IN_PROGRESS -> DONE. completedAt should be populated.
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Patch `
  -Uri "$api/tasks/$taskId" `
  -ContentType "application/json" `
  -Body '{"status":"DONE"}'
